back: Attraction between a lattice of cations and delocalised electrons.

front: Why are metals conductive and malleable?
back: Mobile delocalised electrons carry charge/energy; layers slide while the electron sea holds them.
Higher cation charge (more delocalised electrons) and smaller cation radius.

front: (HL) Why are transition metals hard with high melting points?
back: Delocalised d electrons add to the electron sea; ions are small.

front: Melting point trend Na < Mg < Al?
back: Cation charge increases (+1, +2, +3) and radius decreases, so more delocalised electrons and stronger attraction to the cations.

front: Why do group 1 melting points decrease down the group?
back: Cations get larger, so the delocalised electrons are further from the nucleus and attraction weakens.

front: Why are metals good thermal conductors?
back: Mobile delocalised electrons transfer kinetic energy quickly, along with vibrations of the closely packed cations.

front: Why are metals malleable and ductile but ionic solids brittle?
back: Metallic bonding is non-directional: layers of cations slide without breaking the bonding. In ionic solids sliding brings like charges together.
Delocalised electrons absorb and re-emit light across visible frequencies (reflection).

front: Is a metal lattice made of neutral atoms sharing electrons?
back: No. It is positive ions (cations) in a lattice with delocalised valence electrons; the bond is electrostatic attraction between them.

front: Why is Al a better electrical conductor than Na per atom?
back: Al contributes three delocalised electrons per atom vs one for Na, so more charge carriers.

front: (HL) Which electrons are delocalised in transition metals?
back: Both 4s and 3d electrons, because they are close in energy — giving many delocalised electrons and strong metallic bonding.

front: (HL) Why are transition metals good electrical conductors?
back: They have many delocalised (3d and 4s) electrons that can move through the lattice.

front: Why is copper used for wiring and aluminium for overhead cables?
back: Cu: excellent conductor, ductile. Al: good conductor with low density, so lighter cables (often with a steel core for strength).

front: Why are boiling points of metals much higher than their melting points?
back: Melting only loosens the lattice (metallic bonding persists in the liquid); boiling must separate atoms completely, breaking the metallic bonding.

front: Charge carriers in a metal vs a molten ionic compound?
back: Metal: delocalised electrons move; no chemical change (conducts as a solid). Molten ionic compound: ions move to the electrodes and are discharged (electrolysis).

front: (HL) Why does iron melt at a much higher temperature than calcium?
back: Fe has small cations and many delocalised 3d and 4s electrons; Ca contributes only two 4s electrons per larger cation, so its metallic bonding is weaker.

front: Why can sodium be cut with a knife?
back: Large +1 cations and only one delocalised electron per atom give weak metallic bonding (mp ~98 °C), so it is soft.
